chapter: Youth, the road and arrival in California
title: Banjo Bernie and his first paid gigs in Atlantic City and Philadelphia
summary: He describes a bandleader who rarely paid, a Philadelphia nightclub gig in the Prohibition era, and counts it his first professional work.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Back to school, and after school you went to New York and went to W.C. Handy and went nowhere. Then what happened?

Then... Let's see, I left out a period in Atlantic City when I was still going to school. I ran into a guy... There's always a guy like this in every young musician's life, I guess, who gets the young musicians and doesn't pay them. Banjo Bernie was such a guy. And I used to gig with his band, and he'd promise all kind of things, and some nights we'd get three bucks and some nights nothing. But it was just fun, and I have no regrets; the experience was wonderful. So he took us to Philadelphia, I remember, and we played in a place called the Golden Dawn. It was a nightclub. I don't even remember what street that was on; all I know, it was Philadelphia. And it was chorus girls and everything... This was before whiskey was...liquor

was repealed, so people used to drink booze out of cream pitchers. You had to bring a cream pitcher and some Coca-Cola. I remember getting really out of it a few times, so I figured then "that's not for me." But Banjo Bernie was a real con man. I don't know whatever happened to him. But I just thought I would throw that in, because that was part of my experience.
I guess you would say that was
Well, you did get paid once in a while, so that makes it professional.

Oh, once in a while, yeah. And I didn't have to... You know, my folks fed me, I didn't have to worry too much about money. But just the fact that I was playing... That's why I never...even in school... I forgot about that.
